extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, literary critics, and students of poetics and dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetic dramas (especially tragedy and comedy) according to classical principles: medium, objects and manner of imitation; the components and construction of plot; character, diction, thought, song, and spectacle; and the effects (pity, fear, catharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of Imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different arts differ in the medium of imitation: rhythm, language, and 'harmony' (either singly or combined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate medium for the art: flute/lyre use harmony and rhythm; dancing uses rhythm alone; dramatic poetry may combine metre, language, rhythm and song. Recognize that the medium shapes how imitation is effected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of Imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of imitation are men in action, represented as better than they are, worse than they are, or as they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the moral type appropriate to the genre: tragedy tends to represent men as better than in life, comedy as worse, and other forms may vary. Examples: Homer (men better), Cleophon (as they are), parody authors (worse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of Imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may imitate by narration (speaking in another personality or his own unchanged) or by making the characters live and move before the audience (dramatic presentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide between narrative and dramatic presentation; drama (representation of action) gives different possibilities than mere narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with rhythm, harmony and song; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy must center on a unified action of appropriate seriousness and use poetic devices (song, diction) to produce pity and fear and thereby catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy must have six parts which determine its quality: Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and evaluate each part: Plot and Character are the core; Thought, Diction, Song are artistic means; Spectacle is least artistic and more dependent on stagecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot is the first principle and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy; incidents and the arrangement of incidents (the plot) are the end of a tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize constructing a coherent, causally linked plot. Strong speeches and character portraits cannot substitute for an artistically constructed plot; peripeteia (reversal) and recognition are plot-based devices producing emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as Imitation of Action (not Character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action and of life; life consists in action and its end is a mode of action. Character comes in as subsidiary to actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design characters to serve action; actions—not merely character sketches—determine tragic effect. A sequence of choices and events should drive the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholeness of Plot (Beginning, Middle, End)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole is that which has a beginning, a middle and an end: a beginning does not follow anything by causal necessity; an end naturally follows some other thing and has nothing following it; a middle follows something and has something follow it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the plot's parts are causally and necessarily connected so that the structure feels organic and not haphazard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (Proper Length) of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty depends on magnitude and order: a plot must be of a certain magnitude that can be embraced in one view or by memory; neither too small nor too vast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a length where the sequence of events is perspicuous and the audience can follow the whole; within those limits, larger can be more beautiful, provided order is maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (Single Action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot is not unity of the hero; the plot must imitate one action—structural union such that removing any part disjoints the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sprawling collections of unrelated adventures; center the work on a single coherent action that yields unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry vs History — Universality and Probability
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet relates what may happen (the universal) according to probability or necessity, whereas the historian relates what has happened (the particular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose actions that express general truths about kinds of persons/situations, making events credible by probability or necessity rather than mere coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Epeisodic Plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Epeisodic plots are worst: episodes or acts succeed without probable or necessary sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft causal continuity; avoid stitching together set-pieces or 'show' scenes that do not follow from prior events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex Plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple plots involve change of fortune without reversal (peripeteia) or recognition (anagnorisis). Complex plots include reversal, recognition, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for complex construction (when appropriate) because reversal and recognition—when organically produced—heighten tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of the Situation (Peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change by which the action veers round to its opposite, always subject to probability or necessity (e.g., messenger intended to relieve but reveals a truth producing opposite effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversal that emerges naturally from prior incidents; the effectiveness depends on it feeling necessary or probable rather than accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change from ignorance to knowledge producing love or hate between persons destined to good or bad fortune; best when coincident with reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure recognition so it logically results from earlier events and ideally coincides with reversal to maximize pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene of Suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: A destructive or painful action (death on stage, bodily agony, wounds) that forms part of the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include scenes of suffering when they arise organically and serve the plot; their placement and cause should be narratively justified to produce emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative Parts of Tragedy (Prologue, Episode, Exode, Parode, Stasimon, Commos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into parts: Prologue (before the Chorus' Parode), Episode (between choric songs), Exode (final part with no choric song after it); Choric parts include Parode (first utterance) and Stasimon (choric ode without anapaests/tetrameters); Commos is a lamentation of chorus and actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange these parts to support the plot's progression and to deploy choric and episodic material for thematic and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic Effect by Internal Structure (vs Spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity are best aroused by the inner structure of the piece (plot construction) rather than by spectacular means; producing the effect by spectacle is less artistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plotting and incident design that evoke pity/fear even when the tale is only heard; do not rely primarily on visual shock or monstrous spectacle to produce the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Tragic Subject and Hero (Hamartia Principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should be neither eminently good and just nor an utter villain; misfortune should arise from error or frailty (hamartia) in a person highly renowned and prosperous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity (shocking but not pitiful/fearful) and avoid the downfall of an utter villain (satisfies moral sense but not pity/fear). Aim for a great person whose error induces pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single Issue (Single Catastrophe) Preferred over Double Thread
rubrics_metrics.description: A well constructed plot should be single in its issue rather than double (two opposite catastrophes), which gratifies the weaker desires of spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a single catastrophic resolution to maintain unity and authentic tragic pleasure rather than contrived balance of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relational Context for Tragic Acts (Kinship/Friendship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions that arouse pity and fear typically occur between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent; incidents between those near or dear (kinship, friendship) are especially effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on familial or close relational bonds (father/son, mother/son, brother/brother) to heighten emotional stakes and tragic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Criteria: Goodness, Propriety, Truth-to-life, Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Four aims in character portrayal: (1) goodness (manifest moral purpose), (2) propriety (appropriate traits for sex/status), (3) truth to life, (4) consistency (even consistent inconsistency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft characters whose actions/speeches show moral purpose; ensure traits fit role and social expectations; make characters lifelike and behaviorally consistent. Avoid motiveless degradation or indecorous portrayals and inconsistent transformations without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Intellectual Element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances — where something is proved or a general maxim is enunciated; analogous to rhetoric in speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought to reveal reasoning, values, and to advance argumentation in the drama; it underpins persuasive or revelatory speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and Poetic Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words (the metrical arrangement). Poetic diction combines elevation of language with perspicuity, using rhythm, harmony and song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for language that is elevated yet clear; choose metres and linguistic ornamentation appropriate to tone and part of the play (some parts may be sung, others spoken).

rubrics_metrics.name: Song as Chief Embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the embellishments, Song (choric and lyrical elements) holds the chief place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use song and choric odes to heighten emotional texture and to punctuate and comment on the action, while keeping them integrated with plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle as Least Artistic Element
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle has an emotional attraction but is the least artistic of the parts and is connected least with the art of poetry; spectacular effects depend more on stagecraft than poetic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on spectacular stage effects as a substitute for plot and poetic construction; spectacle should complement, not carry, the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as Maker of Plots (Universality over Particulars)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet ('maker') should be the maker of plots rather than merely a versifier; poetry aims to express the universal (what a person of a certain type will do) rather than the particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus creative energy on constructing archetypal actions and causal structures that express general truths, not just on rhetorical or metrical virtuosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Comedy and the Ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy imitates characters of a lower type; the Ludicrous is a subdivision of the ugly, a defect or ugliness not painful or destructive (e.g., comic mask is ugly but not painful). Comedy aims at representing men as worse than they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In comic writing, exploit defects and the ludicrous (without real harm) and represent lower types to elicit laughter; understand that comedy's aims and criteria differ from tragedy's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Traditional Material with Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets may not destroy received legends but ought to show invention of their own and skilfully handle traditional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt myths and legends creatively: preserve essential framework where necessary but rearrange or invent details to serve dramatic ends and to produce tragedy or comedy effectively.
